newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: British nurses move to stop execution call.
newsitem.headline: British nurses move to stop execution call.

text.p: Two British nurses accused of murdering Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford in Saudi Arabia will take legal action to stop Gilford's family calling for their execution, their Australian lawyer said on Thursday.

Michael Burnett said the South Australian state supreme court will hear an application on Friday seeking to invalidate calls by the victim's brother, Frank Gilford, for the death penalty should the nurses be found guilty.

"We will seek an injunction against Mr Gilford to stop him saying to the court in Saudi Arabia that it is a unanimous view of the family that the death penalty should be inflicted if the nurses are found guilty," Burnett told Reuters.
Burnett said he had been instructed that under Saudi law, the heirs of the dead woman needed to be unanimous in calling for the death penalty.
He said the British nurses would argue that Yvonne's mother Muriel Gilford, who suffers from Alzheimer's disease, is not mentally competent to agree with her son's call for execution.

Sources close to the case told Reuters last month the Kohbar sharia court which is hearing the trial had questioned the power of attorney which Muriel had given her son but had granted him the right to demand execution if the nurses were found guilty.

However the defendants' Saudi law firm, Salah al-Hujailan, later said the court, which is due to resume on August 10, was leaning towards disqualifying the Gilford family from any role in the nurses' fate.

"Upon the demonstration of the mental condition of the mother the court will most probably demand a guardian be appointed by the Australian court," it said in a statement, adding Frank Gilford would not be considered as the guardian.

Yvonne Gilford, 51, was found murdered in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dharhan on December 11 last year, having been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
British nurses Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31, have been charged with murdering Gilford, but have said they are innocent, despite initially signing confessions.
If found guilty the nurses face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword.
According to sharia law the victim's family may demand the death penalty if the court finds the women guilty and says capital punishment is appropriate.
